evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and adolescents with an acute asthma attack in the emergency department. Children are covered in SINA Section 10 (PRAM-based). Verified against the Saudi Initiative for Asthma (SINA) 2024 update.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Local formulary availability and hospital protocol adoption

pathophysiology.summary: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with variable airflow obstruction. In an attack, smooth-muscle bronchospasm, airway wall oedema and mucus plugging narrow the airways, trap air (dynamic hyperinflation) and cause ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
keyMechanisms: Airway narrowing: smooth-muscle contraction, mucosal oedema and increased mucus secretion; chronic remodelling (smooth-muscle hypertrophy, subepithelial fibrosis) adds fixed narrowing.
Type 2 (eosinophilic) inflammation is the commonest pattern (40–70%): IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IgE and mast-cell mediators; usually steroid-responsive.
Early attack: hyperventilation lowers PaCO2. A normal or rising PaCO2 means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

Death in acute asthma: asphyxia from severe obstruction and mucus plugging, severe auto-PEEP reducing venous return and cardiac output, and arrhythmia (risk raised by hypokalaemia and QT prolongation from high-dose beta-agonists).
Most deaths occur in chronically uncontrolled asthma with under-use of inhaled steroids and deterioration over days.

symptoms: Breathlessness, wheeze, chest tightness, cough; increasing reliever use with poor response.
Severe: unable to complete sentences in one breath.
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, accessory muscle use, prolonged expiratory wheeze.
Severe: RR 25 or more (often above 30), HR 120 or more.
Life-threatening: silent chest, cyanosis, weak respiratory effort, bradycardia, arrhythmia, hypotension.
redFlags: Life-threatening features: SpO2 below 92% (PaO2 below 60 mmHg) on high-flow oxygen, PEF below 30%, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, coma, bradycardia, arrhythmia, hypotension, or a NORMAL or HIGH PaCO2
Raised PaCO2 or needs ventilation: near-fatal asthma — ICU
Poor prognostic history: previous near-fatal attack or ICU, admission in the last year, heavy reliever use, not on regular inhaled steroids, psychosocial problems, poor adherence
precipitants: Allergen or irritant exposure; smoking or vaping.
Poor adherence to inhaled steroids; heavy reliever use.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Sudden pleuritic pain, unilateral reduced breath sounds; chest X-ray (mandatory in life-threatening asthma).
Fever, focal crackles, consolidation on X-ray; antibiotics only if bacterial pneumonia is suspected.
Can present like life-threatening asthma; look for trigger exposure, urticaria, angioedema and hypotension — give IM adrenaline.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: On arrival and after each treatment; before discharge
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Moderate: above 50–75% of best or predicted. Severe: 30–50%. Life-threatening: below 30%.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Grades severity and response. Hypercapnia is rare when PEF is 30% or more (or at least 150 L/min).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and start treatment at once
actions: Assess dyspnoea, RR, HR, SpO2 and PEF; classify as moderate, severe or life-threatening (if mixed features, treat as the higher level).
Controlled oxygen to keep SpO2 92% or more; use oxygen-driven nebulisers in severe attacks.
No routine chest X-ray, ABG, antibiotics or sedatives.

clinicalManagement.title: Moderate attack (PEF above 50%)
actions: Salbutamol MDI with spacer 6–12 puffs every 20 min for 1 h, then every 2–4 h; OR nebulised 2.5–5 mg every 20 min for 1 h, then every 2 h.
Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg orally (maximum 50 mg) as soon as possible, for 5–7 days.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe attack (PEF 30–50%, RR 25 or more, HR 120 or more, cannot finish sentences)
actions: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5–5 mg back-to-back every 20 min for 1 h, then hourly.
Add ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised every 20 min for 3 doses, then every 4–6 h (or MDI 4–8 puffs).
IV methylprednisolone 40 mg twice daily (or oral prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg daily, if able to swallow).
Inadequate response: IV magnesium sulphate 1–2 g over 20 min, single dose.
Monitor SpO2; check blood gas if PEF below 30%, electrolytes, glucose and ECG.

clinicalManagement.title: Life-threatening attack
actions: Oxygen to SpO2 92% or more; continuous nebulised salbutamol 10–15 mg with ipratropium 1.5 mg over 1 h (oxygen-driven).
Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 min.
ABG, chest X-ray, electrolytes, glucose, ECG.

clinicalManagement.title: Reassess after 1 h and decide disposition
actions: Adequate: PEF above 60%, SpO2 92% or more on air, stable for at least 4 h → discharge track.

Partial: PEF 30–50%, SpO2 92% or more on oxygen → continue salbutamol + ipratropium every 1–4 h; prednisolone 1 mg/kg (maximum 50 mg) or IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day or methylprednisolone 80 mg/day; admit if no adequate response after 4 h.
Poor: PEF below 30%, SpO2 below 92% on high-flow oxygen, fatigue, rising PaCO2 or respiratory acidosis → ICU.
Needs ventilatory support, falling PEF/FEV1, persisting hypoxia, hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis, exhaustion, shallow breathing or drowsiness.

keyPoints: Grade severity with PEF, RR, HR and SpO2.
Salbutamol back-to-back, controlled oxygen to 92%, steroids early.
Add ipratropium and IV magnesium in severe attacks.
A normal PaCO2 in a severe attack is a danger sign.
Discharge only after 4 h of stable response with an action plan and ICS/LABA.
pitfalls: Routine chest X-ray, ABG or antibiotics.
Discharging without inhaled steroid, inhaler technique check and early follow-up.

patientEducation: Written asthma action plan; inhaler technique with spacer.
Adherence to inhaled steroid/LABA; avoid smoking and vaping.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: ICU for poor responders and life-threatening asthma.
Pulmonary or primary-care follow-up within days.
dischargeCriteria: Adequate response maintained for at least 4 h: PEF above 60% predicted, SpO2 92% or more.
Inhaler technique checked; ICS/LABA prescribed; written action plan given.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Pulmonary or primary-care clinic within a few days; complete oral steroid 5–7 days; review asthma control and adherence.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Increasing symptoms; PEF above 50–75%; no severe features
PEF 30–50%; RR 25 or more; HR 120 or more; cannot complete sentences
SpO2 below 92% on high-flow oxygen; PEF below 30%; silent chest; cyanosis; bradycardia; arrhythmia; hypotension; normal or high PaCO2; exhaustion; confusion; coma
Raised PaCO2 and/or needs mechanical ventilation

regimens.dose: Moderate: MDI 6–12 puffs via spacer, or 2.5–5 mg nebulised, every 20 min for 1 h. Life-threatening: 10–15 mg continuous nebulisation over 1 h
regimens.frequency: Every 20 min for 1 h, then every 1–4 h by response
adjustments: IV salbutamol only if inhaled route fails or is not tolerated

regimens.dose: 0.5 mg nebulised every 20 min for 3 doses, then every 4–6 h (or MDI 4–8 puffs); life-threatening: 1.5 mg with continuous salbutamol over 1 h
adjustments: Benefit shown in severe, not mild–moderate, attacks

regimens.duration: Switch to oral prednisolone when able
